title: Deep Learning Meets ETAS
text:
STATSEI14 · PRACTICAL TUTORIAL


Deep LearningMeets ETAS


Practical Hybrid Workflows for Seismic Forecasting


Francisco Plaza-Vega Universidad de Santiago de Chile


13 October 2026 · Chile


How do we turn a seismic question into a deep-learning experiment?




     



Main idea: A seismic question becomes a deep-learning experiment through explicit choices about information, representation, output and evaluation.
Explain: Use the guiding question to connect the entire tutorial. We begin with seismic observations, define a learning task, introduce how the models combine information, examine research evidence and make the same decisions in a guided practical. ETAS supplies one way to construct a representation. The LSTM remains the core practical example; additional comparisons can use prepared outputs.
Transition: The agenda follows that sequence of scientific decisions, from the question to a weekly occurrence experiment.
Backup: Follow the presentation with the temporal notebook and discussion; use the Transformer comparison if it helps. Adjust the pace to the group.

title: Deep Learning Meets ETAS
section: What can we learn from seismicity?
text:
What can we learn from seismicity?




Signals record ground motion.
Catalogues describe event times, locations and magnitudes.
Histories and maps organize information across time and space.


The same catalogue can support different tasks. First define what the output should mean.


Map: frozen USGS training catalogue and Natural Earth. Illustrates today’s regional setting.


Main idea: Familiar seismic data objects support different scientific questions.
Explain: Begin with what this audience already knows: recorded ground motion, catalogue events and regional histories. A statistical model can also turn a catalogue into an intensity map. These objects support different tasks: detecting an event, estimating a conditional rate, locating a zone of activity or estimating a weekly probability. We choose the quantity of interest and the information available before deciding how a network will use it.
Transition: The same catalogue can support different learning tasks. Our first decision is what we want the output to mean. Read the next examples through their input and task.
Backup: Map from today’s frozen USGS training benchmark with Natural Earth coastlines. It is not the CSN catalogue used in the published case. Observation is incomplete and catalogue records can change.

title: Deep Learning Meets ETAS
section: Deep learning in seismology: inputs and targets
text:
Deep learning in seismology: inputs and targets








Example
Input
Learning task




ConvNetQuake · 2018
Recorded waveforms
Detect events and classify their source region


RECAST · 2023
Past event times and magnitudes
Estimate the next-event time distribution


Delgado et al. · 2025
Features of catalogued events
Classify foreshock, mainshock and aftershock labels


Farfán et al. · 2025
Sequences of daily spatial grids
Forecast gridded seismic activity




Today’s practical: 30 days of history and a seven-day occurrence probability.


Perol et al. · Dascher-Cousineau et al. · Delgado et al. · Farfán et al.


Main idea: Read these applications as different input–target problems, before comparing architectures.
Explain each example: Focus on the observations used and the scientific meaning of the output. Model names are signposts; their mechanisms come next.

ConvNetQuake: a CNN detects events and classifies their source region from recorded waveforms. In our practical, those events are already represented in a catalogue.
RECAST: a recurrent GRU summarizes past event times and magnitudes to model the next-event time distribution. Its benchmark is temporal ETAS. We will use daily inputs and a weekly occurrence target instead.
Delgado et al.: event features support classification after spatial and temporal clustering and labeling. Labels such as foreshock, mainshock and aftershock show why target construction belongs to the scientific problem.
Farfán et al.: sequences of daily 4 × 4 Chilean grids support forecasts of gridded activity. Spatial aggregation anticipates the maps and graphs available after our regional exercise.

Transition: The examples differ because their questions, available information and targets differ. Make those choices explicit before selecting an architecture.
Backup: This selection is not a performance ranking. Event classification does not establish prospective warning. RECAST’s temporal benchmark does not establish superiority over spatial ETAS. Grid labels omit fine epicentre and magnitude information. Sources are linked on the slide.

title: Deep Learning Meets ETAS
section: From a scientific question to a learning task
text:
From a scientific question to a learning task
We define: the question, information available, input and target.
We represent inputs: as a vector, sequence or map.

Represented data → Neural network → Defined output


Compare with a target → Compute a loss → Update weights

Architecture combines information; training adjusts weights.

The output and the loss must match the scientific question.


Main idea: We define the scientific task and representation before selecting an architecture.
Explain: Decide what we want to estimate and what information would be available at that moment. Construct one input and its target, then identify the input’s structure: a vector, sequence or map. Architecture determines how that represented information is combined. A history enters the network, an estimate comes out, and a loss measures its discrepancy from the target. Backpropagation computes gradients, and an optimizer updates the weights. One representation can support several architectures: the same daily history can be flattened for an MLP, scanned by temporal filters or processed recurrently while retaining the target.
Transition: Once the input and target are defined, different architectures provide different ways to combine the available information. Start with nonlinear combinations of a feature vector.
Backup: Validation guides choices and stopping. It does not update weights through backpropagation. Adapted from Units 1 and 2 of the author’s course.

title: Deep Learning Meets ETAS
section: MLP: combine measured features
text:
MLP: combine measured features


A multilayer perceptron learns nonlinear combinations of a feature vector.


Optional extension: the MLP uses 90 values at fixed lag positions. Diagram adapted from the author’s DL course, Unit 2.


Main idea: An MLP combines a vector of measured features through learned layers.
Explain: Follow one connection and then one hidden layer. Weighted combinations and nonlinear activations compose a mapping. This gives the MLP the capacity to learn nonlinear combinations of measured features. In the optional MLP section, flattening the 30 × 3 window gives 90 values, each at a fixed lag position. Whether this capacity helps the scientific task must be evaluated against suitable references.
Transition: The MLP combines values at fixed positions. A CNN adds a different mechanism: a learned local filter reused across positions.
Backup: Flattening preserves fixed lag positions. It does not randomly discard order. The core example is the LSTM, with a Transformer comparison available to support discussion. Diagram provenance: slides/assets/course-adapted/source-map.md.

title: Deep Learning Meets ETAS
section: CNN: learn local patterns with shared filters
text:
CNN: learn local patterns with shared filters


The same filter examines different neighborhoods.


Optional extension: CNN1D shares filters across days. Diagram adapted from the author’s DL course, Unit 3.


Main idea: A convolution applies shared filters to local neighborhoods.
Explain: Use the diagram to identify a local receptive field and shared weights. The capacity comes from reusing a learned detector across local neighborhoods. In the temporal tutorial, CNN1D moves filters across days. In the published case, the CNN processes spatial patterns in ETAS-derived maps. The representation determines what a neighborhood means, and evaluation determines whether those local patterns are useful.
Transition: Local filters combine nearby values. An LSTM offers another way to use an ordered history by repeatedly updating a learned state.
Backup: CNN1D is available for optional exploration after the live comparison. The grid or temporal sampling determines what counts as a neighborhood. No kernel arithmetic is needed here. Diagram adapted from Unit 3 of the author’s course.

title: Deep Learning Meets ETAS
section: LSTM: carry information through a sequence
text:
LSTM: carry information through a sequence


Today’s example: 30 × 3 input → state (16) → Dense + sigmoid → weekly probability


Output: probability of at least one catalogue M ≥ 5 event in the next seven days.
Adapted from the author’s DL course, Unit 4.


Main idea: An LSTM can combine information from earlier and more recent days through a learned state.
Explain: Each blue box contains three daily catalogue features, also called channels: event count transformed as log(1 + count), maximum magnitude excess above 4.5 and event presence. Thirty days form one 30 × 3 input. The LSTM processes that ordered history and builds a final state with 16 values. A Dense layer with a sigmoid converts that state into one probability: at least one catalogue event with M ≥ 5 in the next seven days. Distinguish the 30 observed days, 3 daily features, 16 learned state values and 1 output.
Transition: This is the architecture we will explain in detail in Colab. Its output is one probability. A generative task instead asks for a possible data realization, such as a complete sequence.
Backup: Today’s example uses catalogue events with M ≥ 4.5 to construct the daily features. An empty day has zero count, zero magnitude excess and presence zero. An event exactly at M = 4.5 has zero excess but presence one. The published temporal case uses a different target. Gates and shared weights remain useful background. An optional comparison contrasts recurrence and attention on the same daily tensor.

title: Deep Learning Meets ETAS
section: Generative learning: produce new samples
text:
Generative learning: produce new samples


The output of G is a new data sample, such as a synthetic sequence.


GAN is an adversarial learning scheme; G and D may use different neural architectures.
Later case: mainshock conditions + noise → a possible aftershock sequence.
GAN schematic adapted from the author’s DL course, Unit 5.


Main idea: Generative learning aims to produce data realizations; a GAN trains a generator through an adversarial scheme.
Explain: Follow z into G and stop at the generated sample x̃ = G(z): this is the desired output. The potential contribution is to produce possible realizations of an object, rather than only a point estimate or a class probability. During training, the discriminator compares generated samples with real examples and supplies a signal for improving G. MLP, CNN and LSTM name architectures; a GAN names an adversarial learning scheme whose generator and discriminator can use different architectures. After training, draw new noise and apply G to obtain another possible sample. In the aftershock example, mainshock conditions and noise determine a possible sequence. Generating a sequence and estimating a weekly occurrence probability are different learning tasks.
Transition: We now have the vocabulary to read the research cases in a common order: question, representation, model and output, evidence, and interpretation. Begin with two tasks built from ETAS maps.
Backup: Generative learning describes a task and can use MLP, CNN or recurrent components. A plausible curve alone does not establish a scientifically adequate distribution.

title: Deep Learning Meets ETAS
section: ETAS intensity maps support two learning tasks
text:
ETAS intensity maps support two learning tasks


Nicolis, Plaza & Salas · Spatial Statistics 42 (2021), 100442 · CSN Chile, 2000–2017


Main idea: The first research case uses one statistical representation to define two neural learning tasks.
Explain: Question: how do the size and location of the daily maximum evolve? Representation: begin with catalogue event times, locations and magnitudes. The study fits temporal ETAS across the area and shares its parameters across 1° × 1° grid cells. Evaluate intensity through time to obtain daily maps. Model and output: take the spatial maximum of each map and use 30 values to predict the next maximum with an LSTM; retain 30 maps and use a CNN to classify which of six latitudinal macrozones contains the next maximum. Evidence: inspect the published temporal result after defining these targets. Interpretation: both branches concern summaries of the ETAS-derived field.
Transition: Before reading inputs or results, establish what the representation measures: process intensity, rather than earthquake magnitude or ground shaking.
Backup: Source: Nicolis, Plaza & Salas (2021), pp. 8–9, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.spasta.2020.100442 . This is a temporal ETAS construction with common area-level parameters applied to grid cells. Do not describe it as a jointly fitted spatial ETAS model. The grid here is schematic. Neither neural target identifies the exact next epicentre.

title: Deep Learning Meets ETAS
section: ETAS intensity describes a conditional event rate
text:
ETAS intensity describes a conditional event rate


\lambda(t\mid\mathcal H_t)=\mu+\sum_{t_i<t}\text{contribution from event }i



Background + magnitude-dependent contributions that decay with time

Published construction: common ETAS parameters applied across 1° × 1° cells produce a sequence of intensity maps.

A map value is an estimated occurrence rate, not an earthquake magnitude.


Main idea: The ETAS representation is a conditional event rate built from the catalogue history.
Explain: Past events contribute according to their magnitude and elapsed time. The temporal ETAS parameters are estimated for the study area and shared across grid cells. Evaluating this representation each day creates the maps used by the neural branches. A maximum over cells produces a daily scalar, while retaining the cells preserves spatial structure.
Transition: With the representation defined, make the temporal question precise: what is the maximum of the following day’s map?
Backup: Source: Nicolis, Plaza & Salas (2021), pp. 8–9. The displayed temporal formula is conceptual. The paper’s map construction uses common parameters across cells. Process intensity differs from magnitude, shaking intensity and probability. Converting an event rate into an interval probability requires an explicit predictive calculation.

title: Deep Learning Meets ETAS
section: A map maximum becomes one value in the LSTM input
text:
A map maximum becomes one value in the LSTM input


30 daily spatial maxima → LSTM → next-day maximum intensity


Nicolis, Plaza & Salas (2021) · Original published regression task · Diagram illustrates the operation, not measured values


Main idea: The published LSTM performs regression on a sequence of ETAS intensity maxima.
Explain: Find the largest value in one daily map. Repeat for 30 days to create one input vector. The target is the maximum of the following day’s map. The diagram’s heights and highlighted cell are constructed to explain this operation; they do not reproduce a particular date or forecast. This is a model-derived continuous target. Today’s practical instead uses catalogue channels and a weekly occurrence probability.
Transition: Now read the original published test panel as evidence for that specific regression question.
Backup: Source: Nicolis, Plaza & Salas (2021), pp. 8–10, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.spasta.2020.100442 . The temporal ETAS fit uses area-level parameters across 1° × 1° cells. A spatial maximum retains one value and discards the location and the rest of the field. No empirical 30-day sequence is claimed in this constructed illustration.

Nicolis, Plaza & Salas (2021), Figure 5(b) and Table 3 · Original plotting scale retained


Main idea: The original result shows a fitted sequence and its reported test errors for a specific published setting.
Explain: The green curve labelled Observed in the original panel is the ETAS-derived target. The blue curve is the LSTM prediction. Read the curves before the table: the network follows much of the target’s variation, and its reported RMSE is slightly lower than the ETAS comparison in this magnitude-six setting. R² is a regression measure, not a probability calibration result.
Transition: The same maps support a different question if we retain their spatial structure: which macrozone contains the next maximum?
Backup: Source: Nicolis, Plaza & Salas (2021), Figure 5(b), p. 9, and Table 3, p. 10. Exact M ≥ 6 values: LSTM MSE 0.2804, MAE 0.2136, RMSE 0.5296 and R² 0.6561; ETAS MSE 0.2998, MAE 0.3484, RMSE 0.5475 and R² 0.6241. The source panel’s vertical scale is ambiguous; retain it and do not reinterpret negative plotted values as raw conditional rates. Do not infer dates or associate the panel with the preceding constructed example. At threshold five, ETAS has lower MSE, MAE and RMSE. The paper does not establish that ETAS estimation excluded all test information. These qualifications prevent a claim of uniform neural superiority.

title: Deep Learning Meets ETAS
section: CNN: locate the next map maximum in one of six macrozones
text:
CNN: locate the next map maximum in one of six macrozones


The target is one macrozone containing the next day’s maximum ETAS intensity.


Nicolis, Plaza & Salas (2021), Table 2 · Natural Earth geography · Marker and probabilities are illustrative


Main idea: The CNN classifies the location of a maximum within six predefined latitudinal macrozones.
Explain: Keep the complete spatial map on each of 30 days. The CNN outputs six probabilities that sum to one. The next day’s map supplies one target class: the macrozone containing its maximum. In the constructed example, that maximum is in zone 3. The displayed probability vector is chosen for teaching and is not a fitted prediction. The LSTM asks how large the maximum will be; the CNN asks which macrozone contains it.
Transition: The ETAS case shows how changing the represented information changes the learning task. The next case expands the desired output to an entire possible aftershock sequence.
Backup: Source: Nicolis, Plaza & Salas (2021), Table 2, p. 9, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.spasta.2020.100442 . The geographic figure is reconstructed from the six printed latitudinal bounds, numbered from south to north, and Natural Earth geometry. It is not a source-paper forecast map. The source Table 2 has a 0.01° discrepancy between the fifth and sixth intervals, retained in the diagram data. These six mutually exclusive classes differ from the six marginal cell-occurrence targets in today’s optional map and graph notebooks. They do not identify the exact next epicentre, earthquake magnitude or shaking intensity.

title: Deep Learning Meets ETAS
section: Generative exploration of aftershock sequences
text:
Generative exploration of aftershock sequences


The intended output is a possible sequence conditioned on a mainshock.


Jara Muñoz (2025) · Undergraduate thesis in Statistical Engineering · Universidad de Santiago de Chile


Main idea: The undergraduate thesis explores conditional generation of possible aftershock sequences.
Explain: Question: can a model produce possible aftershock sequences under specified mainshock conditions? Representation: mainshock location, magnitude and depth describe the conditions, and the output contains 224 intervals of 90 minutes over 14 days within 100 km. An occupied interval stores its maximum magnitude; 2.5 marks absence. Model and output: the thesis explores cGAN, WGAN-GP and TGAN, using noise to permit different generated sequences under the same conditions. Illustration: the visible sequence is constructed only to explain the encoding. Interpretation: it is neither an observed catalogue sequence nor the output of a fitted generator; a generated distribution must be assessed through the properties we need it to preserve.
Transition: Move from the representation to evidence: a separate, later manuscript provides an original observed/generated pair for inspection.
Backup: Thesis source: Jara Muñoz (2025), title page and pp. 46–51 (printed pp. 40–45). Mainshock longitude, latitude, magnitude and depth plus derived longitude on a 0–360 scale form five conditioning attributes. The latter is derived, not a fifth independent physical measurement. TGAN is an attention-based generator. The thesis and the later manuscript are separate versions with different evaluations. The shared constructed example has maximum 5.1; it will make binary labels transparent later without representing a fitted result.

title: Deep Learning Meets ETAS
section: An observed and generated sequence: one manuscript case
text:
An observed and generated sequence: one manuscript case


GANT · case B

━━ Generated sequence
Vertical axis: interval maximum magnitude (Mw).
2.5 marks absence.




Compare occurrence, peak magnitude and timing, as well as the shape of the curve.


2026 manuscript under review, Figure 4 · One case from the primary random split · Original PI = −136% for this case


Main idea: A visible pair exposes the properties that a sequence-level score can conceal.
Explain: This is an original observed/generated pair from the manuscript, separate from the preceding constructed example. Both curves share 224 intervals over 336 hours. Identify the long absence periods, the observed isolated peak and the generated activity. An occupied interval stores a maximum magnitude, not an event count. The dark curve is the observed reference; the coral curve is GANT output. Read the original PI annotation as a measure for this one case.
Transition: The next evidence addresses an aggregate property of the representation: occupancy in the separate temporal evaluation.
Backup: Source: Plaza-Vega, Jara, Nicolis & Salinas (2026), manuscript under review, Figure 4, lower-right panel. Case B belongs to the primary random-split experiment. Its PI is −136%, using the original mean-reference denominator. It is neither the random-split aggregate score nor the temporal mean-baseline skill of −13.8%. The cropped panel omits the shared y-axis and legend, which are explicitly supplied on this slide. Empty-bin 2.5 is not an observed magnitude; occupied bins discard within-bin multiplicity. Do not merge this case with the subsequent blocked evaluation or the thesis experiments.

title: Deep Learning Meets ETAS
section: GANT temporal evaluation: too many occupied intervals
text:
GANT temporal evaluation: too many occupied intervals


GANT overproduces occupied intervals while underrepresenting intervals with M ≥ 5.


2026 manuscript under review · Temporal evaluation · Percentages of intervals, not total event counts


Main idea: This GANT configuration does not reproduce two important occupancy properties in the temporal evaluation.
Explain: Read the bars as proportions of all intervals. The generated representation contains far more intervals above the absence marker: 77.43% versus 9.27%. Yet intervals reaching M ≥ 5 are less frequent: 0.40% versus 1.22%. These are distinct errors. A single curve-level loss does not reveal both, and the findings concern this model, representation and evaluation.
Transition: A different question needs a different target: does an observed sequence contain at least one event above a magnitude threshold? That reformulation uses observed outcomes to define labels for separate classifiers.
Backup: In the manuscript’s temporal GANT evaluation, an occupied interval has a value >2.5. Overall occupancy is 9.27% observed and 77.43% generated. Occupancy with M ≥ 5 is 1.22% observed and 0.40% generated. These proportions describe occupied intervals, whose stored maxima discard event multiplicity. Temporal GANT mean-baseline skill is −13.8%. Original PI uses a mean reference, not last-observation persistence. Keep thesis, illustrative cases and blocked results separate. These findings do not establish failure of all generative models.

title: Deep Learning Meets ETAS
section: Observed sequences define magnitude-threshold labels
text:
Observed sequences define magnitude-threshold labels


Mainshock features → classifier → probability of at least one qualifying aftershock


Manuscript under review · 14 days, 100 km · Observed outcomes define labels; the displayed sequence is constructed


Main idea: The manuscript’s classification branch uses observed sequences to define a probability target.
Explain: Question: what is the probability of at least one qualifying aftershock? Representation: mainshock predictors describe the input, while observed catalogue sequences define labels over 14 days within 100 km. Model and output: logistic regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting or XGBoost estimate that probability. Illustration: the constructed sequence makes the labels visible—its maximum is 5.1, so a threshold of five gives label one and a threshold of six gives zero. The classification results follow on the next slide. Interpretation: generated GAN sequences are not classifier inputs, and these are separate binary tasks at each threshold, not multiclass magnitude prediction or a demonstrated improvement to the generator.
Transition: With input and target defined, examine what the reported classification evidence supports under different evaluation schemes.
Backup: Source: Plaza-Vega, Jara, Nicolis & Salinas (2026), manuscript under review, submission version dated 27 April, pp. 4–9 and 18–21. The manuscript uses non-strict magnitude-threshold notation while inherited classification code uses a strict comparison. The constructed maximum 5.1 yields the displayed labels under either convention and therefore does not resolve or hide that source discrepancy. The separate occupancy table on s15 has a confirmed M ≥ 5 definition. The constructed sequence is neither an actual observation nor a fitted GAN output. Do not attribute classification scores to GANs or LSTMs. The temporal analyses split examples by mainshock date, and target windows crossing partition boundaries were not fully purged.
Code verification: The original manuscript repository uses y > threshold in code/analyze_temporal_blocked_validation.py, line 82, and code/analyze_geographic_blocked_validation.py, line 127. Temporal assignment by mainshock date is in code/analyze_temporal_blocked_validation.py, lines 405–411; chronological GANT row splitting is in code/prepare_temporal_blocked_gant_data.py, lines 133–163. Saved metadata confirms target horizons crossing boundaries. This establishes overlapping horizons, not the size of any repeated-event leakage. The separate occupancy calculation uses >= 5.0 in code/build_revision_support_tables.py, lines 480–482.

text:

Each row selects the best model in its own evaluation. Models and evaluation samples differ.

These AUCs measure discrimination. They do not establish calibrated probabilities.


Plaza-Vega, Jara, Nicolis & Salinas (2026), manuscript under review · Table 9 · Magnitude-threshold classification


Main idea: The evaluation protocol matters to the interpretation of classification performance.
Explain: Table 9 concerns at least one aftershock at magnitude threshold six within the encoded 14-day, 100-km horizon. It reports the best classifier under each validation scheme. The random-split result is 0.816 for Random Forest; the temporal result is 0.672 for Gradient Boosting; the geographic result is 0.642 for Random Forest. These are not three evaluations of one fixed fitted model. They indicate more limited discrimination under the blocked schemes in these experiments. ROC-AUC summarizes ranking across thresholds and does not assess calibration of the reported probabilities.
Transition: The cases reveal open questions about representation and evaluation. An ETAS-informed generator is one proposed next experiment, for which results are still needed.
Backup: Source: submission manuscript Table 9, p. 17. The printed target is at least one Mw ≥ 6 aftershock. Inherited classification code uses a strict threshold, as documented on s16. Preserve the different selected models and samples when discussing these values. The study’s target windows crossing temporal partition boundaries were not fully purged. Classifier outputs arise from mainshock features supervised by observed sequence labels. GAN outputs are not the classifier inputs. The magnitude-threshold notation discrepancy described on the preceding slide remains a source limitation. Operational warnings would require additional evaluation and probability calibration evidence.

title: Deep Learning Meets ETAS
section: Research hypothesis: ETAS-informed generation
text:
Research hypothesis: ETAS-informed generation

History available at the origin → ETAS-derived information → Conditional generator

Possible role: supply a conditioning variable or a constraint on generated sequences.
Question: does that addition improve occurrence, magnitude and temporal structure under a fixed evaluation?

This is a proposed research direction. No hybrid results are shown here.


Future work discussed in the manuscript · The tutorial’s illustrative activity score is a separate feature experiment


Main idea: ETAS-informed generation remains a hypothesis that requires its own experiment.
Explain: A statistical process model might supply information to condition a generator or constrain a generated sequence. This is a possible design choice, not an achieved result in the manuscript. A comparison would fit ETAS to the available continuous catalogue, map its information to the same 14-day, 100-km outcome and encoding, and retain an unchanged generative reference. It would evaluate occurrence, magnitude and temporal structure under the same protocol.
Transition: Across these studies, the recurring decisions concern the question, representation, output and evidence. The practical will make those same decisions explicit in a smaller regional forecasting experiment.
Backup: The manuscript discusses ETAS and hybrid ETAS–machine-learning work as future directions on p. 21. No empirical ETAS–GAN performance is claimed. Any ETAS fit and derived information must respect the information available at each origin. A fitted ETAS intensity is a conditional event rate; the illustrative truncated activity score in the tutorial has a different status. A future two-part neural model for occurrence and conditional magnitude also remains unvalidated.

Main idea: The practical applies the same scientific decisions, with a new and explicit regional occurrence target.
Explain: Across these studies, the key decisions were how to represent available information, define an output with scientific meaning, select a model and evaluate the result. The table shows how those decisions lead to different tasks. We will now make them explicit using 30 days of catalogue history to estimate the probability of at least one M ≥ 5 event during the following seven days. The practical’s continuity with the studies lies in this modelling process, rather than in reproducing their targets or results.
Transition: First turn the catalogue into three daily features and inspect one input and its future label. Then fit simple references and the LSTM, and interpret its probability scores. Optional comparisons can extend the discussion.
Backup: Today’s task does not reproduce the research studies. The guided sequence is one example, references, LSTM fitting and evaluation. Transformer results can be read from prepared outputs. CNN maps offer a spatial contrast. Introduce Graph + LSTM through its input and output; its full fitting procedure is optional further exploration. Keep prepared results available if setup or fitting stalls.

title: Deep Learning Meets ETAS
section: From the catalogue to three daily features
text:
From the catalogue to three daily features
For each day, summarize catalogue events with M ≥ 4.5 inside the study region.








Daily feature
Definition
What it describes




Event count
log(1 + N_t)
How many input events occurred


Maximum magnitude excess
Maximum magnitude − 4.5; zero if empty
How far the maximum exceeds 4.5


Event presence
1 if N_t > 0; otherwise 0
Whether any input event occurred



30 consecutive days (rows) × 3 daily features (columns) → one LSTM input
Illustrative day: two input events, maximum M = 5.2 → [1.10, 0.70, 1] before standardization.

Input: 30 past days, M ≥ 4.5 → output: probability of at least one M ≥ 5 event in the next seven days.


The table shows values before standardization. The network uses means and standard deviations from training histories only. Features are also called channels.


Main idea: Three daily catalogue features form the columns of one 30-day input matrix.
Explain: For each day, count catalogue events with M ≥ 4.5 inside the study region: this is N_t. The first feature is the natural logarithm log(1 + N_t). The second subtracts 4.5 from that day’s maximum input magnitude, assigning zero on an empty day. The third is one when N_t is positive and zero otherwise. Two qualifying events and a maximum of 5.2 give [log(3), 5.2 − 4.5, 1], approximately [1.10, 0.70, 1] before standardization. Repeat for 30 consecutive past days to obtain rows × columns = 30 × 3. Features and channels refer to those same three columns. The output is the probability of at least one catalogue M ≥ 5 event in the next seven days; its observed label is zero or one.
Transition: How should these input histories and future labels be divided for learning and evaluation?
Backup: Region: 28–34°S, 69–74°W. Forecast origins are Mondays. Arrays use examples × days × features. The MLP, CNN1D, LSTM and Transformer share the same 30 × 3 history in the temporal comparison. Presence is redundant with count: it equals one whenever count is positive. It distinguishes an empty day from a day with an event exactly at M = 4.5 if one examines magnitude excess alone, because both have zero excess. No performance gain from adding presence has been demonstrated here. Training histories determine each feature’s standardization mean and standard deviation; the numerical example precedes that transformation. The example is constructed for explanation. ComCat mixes magnitude scales. The thresholds are teaching choices, not proof of completeness. The target does not specify exact location, shaking or damage.

title: Deep Learning Meets ETAS
section: Optional comparison: a Transformer on the same history
text:
Optional comparison: a Transformer on the same history


Same history and target. A different way to combine information across days.


Current temporal tutorial · 2,257 trainable parameters versus 1,297 for LSTM · One fixed, small configuration


Main idea: Attention combines the same observed days differently from an LSTM state.
Explain: If the pace allows a brief comparison, show the temporal notebook’s Transformer using prepared outputs. Each day is projected to 16 features and receives a learned 16-value day-position embedding. Two attention heads, each with key dimension 8, combine positions. Residual additions and layer normalization surround attention and the 16-to-16 feed-forward sublayer. Average pooling and a sigmoid produce the weekly probability.
Transition: Compare the probabilities under the unchanged evaluation.
Backup: The Transformer first projects each day and adds a learned position vector. Projection: 64 parameters, learned positions: 480, attention: 1,088, two normalizations: 64, feed-forward: 544, output: 17. Total: 2,257 trainable parameters versus 1,297 for LSTM. No dropout is applied. All input positions precede the origin, so within-history attention does not expose the target. Capacity differs between architectures. Attention weights alone do not establish causation.

text:
Spatial extension: Graph + LSTM


Graph connections share spatial information; the LSTM summarizes each node’s history.


Input/output introduction · Complete graph example for optional exploration


Main idea: Graph + LSTM keeps the same six cells as the map example and separates spatial from temporal operations.
Explain: Point to the six geographic cells, which are nodes rather than individual earthquakes. Each node contains 30 days of three catalogue features. Within a day, graph convolution combines features over fixed rook adjacency. A shared LSTM processes the sequence for each node, and a sigmoid head produces one weekly occurrence probability per cell. Several cells can be positive in the same week, so these marginal probabilities need not sum to one.
Transition: These examples suggest possible research questions about representation, available information and evaluation, rather than a universal ranking of architectures.
Backup: This slide introduces input and output. The complete Graph + LSTM notebook is optional further exploration. Geographic adjacency is a modelling choice and does not establish physical triggering. The implementation includes the focal node in the neighborhood average and learns a separate self-transformation. Compare identity adjacency under unchanged inputs and protocol to investigate the role of cross-node messages. Map and graph scores concern the same cell-level target and should not be ranked against regional occurrence scores.

Appendix · the LSTM steps
Input: 30 days × 3 channels. Output: one weekly occurrence probability.
inputs = keras.Input(shape=(30, 3))
state = keras.layers.LSTM(16)(inputs)
probability = keras.layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")(state)
model_lstm = keras.Model(inputs, probability)
model_lstm.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="binary_crossentropy")
history_lstm = model_lstm.fit(
    X_train, y_train, validation_data=(X_val, y_val),
    epochs=20, batch_size=64, callbacks=[stopping_lstm], shuffle=False)
p_lstm = model_lstm.predict(X_val).ravel()
brier = np.mean((p_lstm - y_val) ** 2)

Define the model · compile · fit · predict · evaluate probabilities


Abbreviated reference for the guided practical. The same compile, fit, predict and probability-evaluation workflow applies to the supervised MLP and CNN1D examples; each requires its own model, stopping callback and fitted history. These steps do not replace the alternating GAN updates. The notebook sets seed 7 and prepares training-only scaling. Beside compile, it defines stopping_lstm with patience 3 and restored best weights. The notebook specifies Adam learning rate 0.001 explicitly. Validation selects stopping rather than updating weights through gradients. Each operation appears next to the model it concerns. https://keras.io/api/layers/recurrent_layers/lstm/ .

title: Further exploration
section: Questions to take into your research
text:
Questions to take into your research

Which aspects of seismic activity does the input representation retain, and which does it leave out?
What information would actually be available when issuing a forecast?
Does a model improve on a simple reference, and does that conclusion depend on the metric or initialization?
Which additional data or evaluation period would support a stronger conclusion?

The validation table and calibration outputs in the temporal guide illustrate these questions. An observed difference between models can suggest a hypothesis; it does not by itself identify the reason for that difference.

title: Further exploration

text:
Two short research examples
The research examples connect the case studies to explicit inputs and targets. Inspect how daily maps become one temporal window, then how an aftershock sequence becomes a threshold label. These are short data transformations with prepared outputs, rather than another training exercise.

title: Further exploration
section: Read across scientific tasks
text:
Read across scientific tasks
The references include forecasting studies such as RECAST and Farfán et al., and detection or classification studies such as ConvNetQuake and Delgado et al. A useful way to connect them to your own work is to compare their questions, representations and evidence.








Aspect
Question for reading a study

What question does the model answer?


Input and information availability
What is one input example, and when are its measurements available?


Target
What is predicted, over which horizon and spatial support?


Evaluation
Which splits, reference forecasts and metrics support the claim?


Limits
What is unresolved or not reported in the source consulted?




A retrospectively assigned foreshock/mainshock/aftershock label differs from a prospective forecasting target. Scores for different tasks cannot be ranked directly. When reusing a claim, cite the source and distinguish evidence available in its full text from information in an abstract. The Jara thesis and the manuscript under review are separate sources.

title: Further exploration
section: Explore the supplied models
text:
Explore the supplied models
The optional MLP and CNN1D sections of the temporal notebook follow the LSTM and Transformer. They process the same 30 × 3 input using different assumptions: fixed lag positions in an MLP, shared temporal filters in CNN1D, recurrent state in an LSTM, and learned positions plus attention in the Transformer.
Each model places its definition, compile, fit, predict and evaluation together. This makes it possible to follow what training changes and which settings the researcher chooses beforehand. Parameter counts and completed epochs provide context for the losses.
The guided examples use seed 7. The separate three-seed comparison, also available as a notebook, explores seeds 7, 17 and 27. Read Brier score, log loss and calibration alongside the simple references. Mean losses summarize individually scored fits; they are not the loss of an ensemble prediction. A single run cannot establish stability across initializations.
See Environment and setup for software versions and the context of the prepared results. If you rerun a notebook, recording your versions and hardware helps interpret numerical differences.

title: Further exploration
section: One optional experiment: 8, 16 and 32 LSTM units
text:
One optional experiment: 8, 16 and 32 LSTM units
The network learns weights and biases. Its recurrent-state size is a setting chosen before fitting. The 16-unit LSTM is a compact starting configuration; this tutorial does not establish it as optimal.
If model capacity is relevant to your research question, a controlled comparison could use the following protocol:

Declare 8, 16 and 32 units before fitting. Change only the number in keras.layers.LSTM(16) in a separate copy of the temporal notebook.
Keep the three channels, 30-day history, target, region, chronological partitions, training-only scaling, Adam learning rate 0.001, batch size 64, maximum 20 epochs and patience 3 fixed. Keep restore_best_weights=True and shuffle=False.
Declare validation log loss as the primary comparison; also inspect Brier score, calibration with bin counts, parameter count and completed epochs. Seed 7 provides an initial walkthrough; assessing initialization sensitivity requires repeating every candidate with seeds 7, 17 and 27.
Retain every run, including neutral or worse results. Examine whether a difference persists across these initializations, rather than selecting the best-looking seed.

The seven-day horizon and M ≥ 5 threshold define the scientific target. Changing them studies a different outcome. Changing the seed studies another training realization; it does not create new earthquake observations.
Validation controls early stopping and the comparison of candidates. A selected validation score remains development evidence. Independent assessment requires data that did not influence these choices and a selection procedure that respects chronological order.

title: Further exploration
section: Continue with Graph + LSTM
text:
Continue with Graph + LSTM
The graph tutorial starts with a study-area map and overlays the numbered six-cell grid before representing those cells as nodes. Follow the sequence at your own pace: inspect the cells and their neighbours, read one 30 × 6 × 3 input, then trace neighbour aggregation and the LSTM to six weekly occurrence probabilities. The notebook and its example outputs are complete even if the live discussion stops at the representation.
Compare the graph with the map tutorial using the same cells and targets. The six probabilities describe separate cell outcomes and need not sum to one. They differ from the six mutually exclusive macrozone classes in Nicolis et al. (2021).

title: Further exploration
section: Keep an exploration interpretable
text:
Keep an exploration interpretable
For any experiment you choose to pursue, define the hypothesis and proposed change before fitting. Keep an unchanged reference and save new outputs separately. A reproducible record includes the model settings, data provenance, software environment and every declared run.
Brier score, log loss and calibration describe complementary aspects of probability forecasts. Common calibration bins and their counts help compare models and seeds. Retaining all seeds distinguishes a recurring difference from a favourable individual fit; those seeds are not additional independent earthquake weeks.
Use training and validation for these explorations. The 2021–2025 test period was inspected in earlier work and cannot serve as a new untouched test for selecting a configuration. A confirmatory follow-up needs a new evaluation period and a protocol fixed before examining its outcomes. Revised catalogue records also do not establish what was available at historical forecast times.

title: A catalogue history becomes a probability forecast
section: Preparation C. Select the region and define the daily calendar
text:
Preparation C. Select the region and define the daily calendar
Input events satisfy M ≥ 4.5. The future occurrence target uses M ≥ 5. We retain every calendar day, including days without events. The first year supplies history for the earliest training windows.
We will summarize each day with three daily catalogue features: measured variables that are also called channels. This is a representation chosen for this exercise, not a requirement that a neural network must have three inputs. The next section defines each feature before we construct it.

Code block 5 · Run the matching prepared-notebook cell in order. For self-study, copy into a new Colab code cell.

START = pd.Timestamp("2000-01-01", tz="UTC")
END = pd.Timestamp("2026-01-01", tz="UTC")
days = pd.date_range(START, END - pd.Timedelta(days=1), freq="D")
FEATURES = ["log_count", "max_magnitude_excess", "has_event"]

inside = events["latitude"].between(-34.0, -28.0)
inside &= events["longitude"].between(-74.0, -69.0)
in_time = (events["time"] >= START) & (events["time"] < END)
selected = events.loc[inside & in_time & (events["mag"] >= 4.5)].copy()
selected["date"] = selected["time"].dt.floor("D")
print("Input events:", len(selected))

title: A catalogue history becomes a probability forecast
section: Preparation D. Build three regional columns
text:
Preparation D. Build three regional columns
Grouping counts the events on each day. Reindexing inserts the missing days. The separate target count will only be used to form outcomes after a forecast origin.

Code block 6 · Run the matching prepared-notebook cell in order. For self-study, copy into a new Colab code cell.

daily_count = selected.groupby("date").size().reindex(days, fill_value=0)
daily_count = daily_count.to_numpy(dtype="float32")

daily_maximum = selected.groupby("date")["mag"].max().reindex(days)
daily_excess = (daily_maximum - 4.5).fillna(0).to_numpy(dtype="float32")

larger_events = selected.loc[selected["mag"] >= 5.0]
target_counts = larger_events.groupby("date").size().reindex(days, fill_value=0)
target_counts = target_counts.to_numpy(dtype="float32")

daily_regional_raw = np.column_stack([
    np.log1p(daily_count),
    daily_excess,
    (daily_count > 0).astype("float32"),
]).astype("float32")
daily_table = pd.DataFrame(daily_regional_raw, index=days, columns=FEATURES)
assert daily_count.sum() == len(selected)
display(daily_table.head(10))

title: A catalogue history becomes a probability forecast
section: Preparation E. One Monday becomes one learning example
text:
Preparation E. One Monday becomes one learning example
At origin t, take inputs from [t − 30 days, t) and the outcome from [t, t + 7 days). The Python slices below implement those intervals directly. We omit target weeks that cross a partition boundary.
Only origins through 2020 are built. Weekly targets do not overlap, although input histories share days.

Code block 7 · Run the matching prepared-notebook cell in order. For self-study, copy into a new Colab code cell.

VAL_START = pd.Timestamp("2017-01-01", tz="UTC")
TEST_START = pd.Timestamp("2021-01-01", tz="UTC")
candidate_origins = pd.date_range("2001-01-01", "2020-12-31", freq="W-MON", tz="UTC")

histories, outcomes, kept_origins = [], [], []
for origin in candidate_origins:
    i = days.get_loc(origin)
    target_end = origin + pd.Timedelta(days=HORIZON)
    boundary = VAL_START if origin < VAL_START else TEST_START
    if i < LOOKBACK or target_end > boundary:
        continue

    history = daily_regional_raw[i - LOOKBACK:i]
    future_counts = target_counts[i:i + HORIZON]
    outcome = int(future_counts.sum() > 0)
    histories.append(history)
    outcomes.append(outcome)
    kept_origins.append(origin)

origins = pd.DatetimeIndex(kept_origins)
raw_regional = np.stack(histories)
y_regional = np.asarray(outcomes, dtype="int32")
train_mask = origins < VAL_START
val_mask = origins >= VAL_START

assert (origins[train_mask] + pd.Timedelta(days=HORIZON) <= VAL_START).all()
assert (origins[val_mask] + pd.Timedelta(days=HORIZON) <= TEST_START).all()
print("Training examples:", train_mask.sum(), "Validation examples:", val_mask.sum())
print("One input:", raw_regional[0].shape, "One outcome:", y_regional[0])

title: A catalogue history becomes a probability forecast
section: Preparation F. Estimate scaling from training histories
text:
Preparation F. Estimate scaling from training histories
Estimate one mean and one standard deviation per daily catalogue feature from the training windows. A historical day can contribute to several overlapping windows. Apply these training estimates to all validation histories. Validation has no role in estimating the scaling parameters.
The three-feature examples above are raw values. Standardization subtracts the training mean and divides by the training standard deviation: (value - training_mean) / training_std. A negative standardized value means that the feature value is below its training mean; it does not mean a negative earthquake magnitude. A raw zero can therefore become negative when the training mean is positive. The feature meanings and their order stay the same.

Code block 8 · Run the matching prepared-notebook cell in order. For self-study, copy into a new Colab code cell.

regional_mean = raw_regional[train_mask].mean(axis=(0, 1), dtype=np.float64)
regional_scale = raw_regional[train_mask].std(axis=(0, 1), dtype=np.float64)
regional_scale = np.where(regional_scale > 0, regional_scale, 1.0)
X_regional = ((raw_regional - regional_mean) / regional_scale).astype("float32")
assert np.isfinite(X_regional).all()

display(pd.DataFrame({
    "channel": FEATURES, "training_mean": regional_mean, "training_sd": regional_scale
}))

title: A catalogue history becomes a probability forecast
section: 2. Fit two reference forecasts
text:
2. Fit two reference forecasts
The first forecast always returns the training positive fraction. Logistic regression uses all 90 lagged values, in the same order as the MLP below. Neither reference is tuned on validation.
Flattening preserves a fixed position for each day and feature. It does not randomly reorder the history.

Code block 10 · Run the matching prepared-notebook cell in order. For self-study, copy into a new Colab code cell.

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

training_prevalence = float(y_train.mean())
p_prevalence = np.full(len(y_val), training_prevalence)

X_train_flat = X_train.reshape(len(X_train), LOOKBACK * len(FEATURES))
X_val_flat = X_val.reshape(len(X_val), LOOKBACK * len(FEATURES))

logistic = LogisticRegression(C=1.0, solver="lbfgs", max_iter=2000)
logistic.fit(X_train_flat, y_train)
assert logistic.n_iter_.max() < logistic.max_iter, "Inspect convergence."
p_logistic = logistic.predict_proba(X_val_flat)[:, 1]

print("Constant probability:", round(training_prevalence, 4))
print("Logistic regression input:", X_train_flat.shape)

title: A catalogue history becomes a probability forecast
section: 3. LSTM: update a learned state through the history
text:
3. LSTM: update a learned state through the history
Input: 30 days × 3 daily catalogue features (channels). Each day contains log(1 + event count), maximum magnitude excess above 4.5, and an event indicator. The LSTM reads the oldest day first and the most recent day last.
The final LSTM state contains 16 learned features. A Dense layer with a sigmoid activation transforms it into one probability of at least one catalogue M ≥ 5 event in the following seven days:
30 × 3 input → final state (16 values) → Dense + sigmoid → weekly probability.
The state starts again for each history. It is not carried between training examples or into validation.
Discuss: Which quantities describe observed inputs, which describe the internal representation, and which describe the model output?

Code block 11 · Run the matching prepared-notebook cell in order. For self-study, copy into a new Colab code cell.

keras.backend.clear_session()
keras.utils.set_random_seed(SEED)

inputs = keras.Input(shape=X_train.shape[1:], name="history")
history_state = keras.layers.LSTM(16, stateful=False, name="read_history")(inputs)
probability = keras.layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid", name="weekly_probability")(history_state)
model_lstm = keras.Model(inputs, probability, name="LSTM")
model_lstm.summary()

The network learns weights and biases from the training data. We specify the architecture and training settings before fitting.

compile sets the optimizer and binary cross-entropy loss. fit adjusts the weights using the training examples. Early stopping monitors validation loss; restore_best_weights=True keeps the weights from the epoch with the lowest validation loss. predict applies those fitted weights to the validation histories.
Validation observations do not supply the gradient updates, but their loss influences which weights are retained. The validation scores therefore describe model development.
These values provide a compact starting configuration for the exercise. They have not been established as optimal by a hyperparameter search. Every neural model uses the same Adam learning rate, batch size, epoch limit and stopping rule; parameter counts differ.
The seven-day horizon and M ≥ 5 threshold define the scientific question. Changing them changes the target. The seed identifies a training realization, not a parameter to optimize for the most favourable score.
Optional exploration: compare 8, 16 and 32 LSTM units with the data and remaining settings fixed, following “Optional exploration: sensitivity to recurrent-state size” below.

    X_train, y_train,
    validation_data=(X_val, y_val),
    epochs=EPOCHS, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE,

4. Evaluate the LSTM against the references
First compare probability forecasts for the same validation weeks. Brier score is the mean squared probability error; log loss also penalizes confident incorrect forecasts. Lower is better for both. Validation also selected the stopping epoch, so this is a development comparison.
The following calculation uses the two references and the LSTM only. You can inspect this complete comparison before introducing attention. The seed is recorded only for a neural fit.

assert np.isfinite(predicted_lstm).all()
assert ((predicted_lstm >= 0) & (predicted_lstm <= 1)).all()

safe_lstm = np.clip(predicted_lstm, 1e-7, 1 - 1e-7)
logloss_before_attention = -(observed * np.log(safe_lstm)
    + (1 - observed) * np.log1p(-safe_lstm)).mean(axis=0)
comparison_lstm = pd.DataFrame({
    "model": probabilities_lstm.columns,
    "seed": [None, None, SEED],
    "brier": brier_before_attention,
    "log_loss": logloss_before_attention,
})

You have mapped the training catalogue, represented 30 days as a 30 × 3 array, and evaluated an LSTM probability against two references, and read calibration alongside the number of weeks supporting each point. This is the stopping point for the live practical.

title: A catalogue history becomes a probability forecast
section: Optional extension. Transformer: combine days through attention and position
text:
Optional extension. Transformer: combine days through attention and position
The input and target stay fixed. Each day is first represented by 16 features. The DayPosition layer adds a trainable vector for each of the 30 lags, allowing the model to distinguish where an observation occurs within the input history.
The position table has shape 30 × 16. Attention then combines information across the observed days.

Code block 17 · Run the matching prepared-notebook cell in order. For self-study, copy into a new Colab code cell.

class DayPosition(keras.layers.Layer):
    def build(self, input_shape):
        self.positions = self.add_weight(
            name="positions",
            shape=(int(input_shape[1]), int(input_shape[2])),
            initializer=keras.initializers.RandomNormal(stddev=0.02),
            trainable=True,
        )
        super().build(input_shape)

    def call(self, inputs):
        return inputs + self.positions

Follow the represented history through one attention block
All 30 input days precede the forecast origin. Attention across this complete input window therefore does not access the future target. Positional vectors distinguish different lags. Residual additions and normalization preserve and refine the represented history.
The final pooling and sigmoid produce the same scalar weekly probability as the other models. Attention weights by themselves would not establish a physical triggering mechanism.

Code block 18 · Run the matching prepared-notebook cell in order. For self-study, copy into a new Colab code cell.

keras.backend.clear_session()
keras.utils.set_random_seed(SEED)

inputs = keras.Input(shape=X_train.shape[1:], name="history")
projected_days = keras.layers.Dense(16, name="project_day")(inputs)
positioned_days = DayPosition(name="day_positions")(projected_days)

attention = keras.layers.MultiHeadAttention(
    num_heads=2, key_dim=8, dropout=0.0, name="attention"
)(positioned_days, positioned_days)
attended_days = keras.layers.Add(name="attention_residual")([positioned_days, attention])
attended_days = keras.layers.LayerNormalization(epsilon=1e-6, name="attention_norm")(attended_days)

feed_forward = keras.layers.Dense(16, activation="relu", name="ff_hidden")(attended_days)
feed_forward = keras.layers.Dense(16, name="ff_output")(feed_forward)
refined_days = keras.layers.Add(name="ff_residual")([attended_days, feed_forward])
refined_days = keras.layers.LayerNormalization(epsilon=1e-6, name="ff_norm")(refined_days)

history_summary = keras.layers.GlobalAveragePooling1D(name="pool_days")(refined_days)
probability = keras.layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid", name="weekly_probability")(history_summary)
model_transformer = keras.Model(inputs, probability, name="Transformer")
model_transformer.summary()

Each column below contains predictions for the same validation origins. We calculate both scores directly, over rows. Log loss penalizes confident incorrect probabilities strongly. Clipping is only for the logarithms; Brier uses the original probabilities.

title: A catalogue history becomes a probability forecast
section: 7. Inspect learning curves
text:
7. Inspect learning curves
The curves show how training and validation loss changed during fitting. Predictions above use the restored best weights; the history still includes all executed epochs. The limit of 20 epochs is a maximum: early stopping can end training sooner. Reaching that limit does not establish that the training budget is adequate.
In the supplied seed-7 run, the LSTM reaches 20 epochs, with its lowest validation loss at epoch 20. The Transformer stops after six epochs and restores the weights from epoch 3. Validation loss therefore affects which fitted weights are used for prediction, even though validation observations do not supply gradient updates.
Discuss: Which epoch has the lowest validation loss for each model? Did either run reach the maximum? Did the more complex model improve on the constant reference? A single run cannot establish an architecture ranking.

    epoch = np.arange(1, len(fitted_history.history["loss"]) + 1)
    axes[0].plot(epoch, fitted_history.history["loss"], label=name)
    axes[1].plot(epoch, fitted_history.history["val_loss"], label=name)
axes[0].set(title="Training", xlabel="Epoch", ylabel="Log loss")
axes[1].set(title="Validation", xlabel="Epoch", ylabel="Log loss")
axes[1].legend()

section: Reflect on the optional Transformer comparison
text:
Reflect on the optional Transformer comparison
You have turned one 30 × 3 history into a probability, evaluated that probability against two references, and changed the architecture while preserving the input and outcome. This completes the optional architecture comparison.
Ask: did the individual neural runs improve both scores, and what would be needed for an independent assessment? One seed does not measure initialization variability; validation is also used for early stopping. An untouched evaluation period and a predeclared protocol would be needed for a new assessment.

Optional exploration: sensitivity to recurrent-state size

Declare the candidates before fitting: 8, 16 and 32 LSTM units.
Keep the daily catalogue features, 30-day history, target, chronological partitions, scaling, optimizer, batch size and stopping rule fixed.
Predeclare validation log loss as the main comparison criterion, and report Brier score and calibration with their sample counts.
First inspect one run per candidate with seed 7. Then repeat every candidate with seeds 7, 17 and 27, retaining each run and summarizing all three seeds. Do not select the best-looking seed.
Examine whether any improvement with capacity is consistent under this protocol. Variation across seeds describes training sensitivity, not uncertainty from a new catalogue.

Candidate selection uses validation information, so the best validation score remains evidence for model development. A future independent assessment requires data that did not influence these choices and a protocol that respects chronological order. The already inspected 2021–2025 period is not a new independent test.
Other extensions: continue with MLP/CNN1D below, daily maps, the six-cell graph, or sensitivity to initialization.

title: A catalogue history becomes a probability forecast
section: Extension B. CNN1D: apply shared filters to adjacent days
text:
Extension B. CNN1D: apply shared filters to adjacent days
A filter of width three examines three neighbouring days and all three daily catalogue features (input channels). The second convolution combines these local responses. Global average pooling summarizes the responses over the window.
This convolution moves over time, not over geographic cells. Pooling makes the final representation less sensitive to exact lag positions.
Discuss: What might happen if the same short pattern occurs five days earlier in the history?

keras.utils.set_random_seed(SEED)

inputs = keras.Input(shape=X_train.shape[1:], name="history")
local_patterns = keras.layers.Conv1D(
    16, kernel_size=3, padding="same", activation="relu", name="local_patterns"
)(inputs)
combined_patterns = keras.layers.Conv1D(
    16, kernel_size=3, padding="same", activation="relu", name="combined_patterns"
)(local_patterns)
history_summary = keras.layers.GlobalAveragePooling1D(name="pool_days")(combined_patterns)
probability = keras.layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid", name="weekly_probability")(history_summary)
model_cnn1d = keras.Model(inputs, probability, name="CNN1D")
model_cnn1d.summary()

title: Two research examples: inputs and targets
section: A. A map maximum becomes a temporal input
text:
A. A map maximum becomes a temporal input
In Nicolis, Plaza and Salas (2021), the LSTM receives 30 daily spatial maxima of an ETAS-derived intensity representation. Here we construct small arrays to make that operation visible. These values are not fitted ETAS outputs or earthquake observations. The six cells keep the example short; they are not the six published macrozone classes.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Construct 31 small daily maps
Each map has three rows and two columns. A deliberately fixed spatial pattern makes the temporal operation easy to inspect. Day numbers have no correspondence with dates in the published catalogue. The intensity scale is illustrative and uses arbitrary units.
activity = np.array([
    0.8, 0.7, 0.9, 1.0, 0.8, 0.6, 0.7, 1.2, 1.8, 1.4,

title: Two research examples: inputs and targets
section: B. A sequence becomes a magnitude-threshold label
text:
B. A sequence becomes a magnitude-threshold label
The submitted manuscript derives classifier targets from observed aftershock outcomes within 100 km and 14 days of a mainshock. The predictors describe the mainshock. Generated GAN samples are not the source of the classifier labels.
The following constructed reference sequence illustrates that observed-outcome representation. It has 224 intervals of 90 minutes (14 days), with 2.5 marking absence and a maximum magnitude in an occupied interval. Its values are the same teaching illustration used in the slides; they are not an observed catalogue sequence or a fitted generator output.
sequence = np.full(224, 2.5)
occupied_bins = [12, 34, 61, 87, 108, 146, 190, 219]
sequence[occupied_bins] = [4.1, 3.4, 5.1, 4.2, 3.1, 4.6, 3.8, 4.0]

threshold = 5.0  # Change to 6.0 to ask a different question.
qualifying_bins = sequence >= threshold
label = int(qualifying_bins.any())
assert sequence.shape == (224,)
assert [int((sequence >= value).any()) for value in [5.0, 6.0]] == [1, 0]
print("Maximum magnitude:", sequence.max())
print("At least one interval with M >=", threshold, ":", label)
Maximum magnitude: 5.1
At least one interval with M >= 5.0 : 1

for threshold in [5.0, 6.0]:
    label = int((sequence >= threshold).any())
    print(f"Threshold {threshold:.1f}: label {label}")

days_after_mainshock = np.arange(224) * 90 / (24 * 60)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.4))
ax.plot(days_after_mainshock, sequence, color="#087e8b", linewidth=1, label="Constructed reference sequence")
ax.axhline(5, color="#d86720", linestyle="--", label="Threshold 5: label 1")
ax.axhline(6, color="#756cc7", linestyle=":", label="Threshold 6: label 0")
ax.set(xlabel="Days after mainshock", ylabel="Maximum magnitude / absence code",
       xlim=(0, 14), ylim=(2.3, 6.3), title="One sequence, two occurrence questions")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper right")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
Threshold 5.0: label 1
Threshold 6.0: label 0

Open full-size figure
Read the example: changing the threshold changes the scientific target. The binary label retains whether a qualifying interval exists and discards its timing, multiplicity and most of the trajectory. A supervised classifier needs many real mainshock-feature/observed-label pairs and a declared evaluation protocol.
This illustration follows the manuscript’s written non-strict threshold definition. Some inherited classification scripts use a strict comparison instead. The illustrative maximum 5.1 gives the same two labels with either operator, but does not resolve that implementation discrepancy or reproduce its empirical labels. The separate occupancy comparison in the slides has its own verified threshold definition.

section: Connect the examples to the practical
text:
Connect the examples to the practical
The temporal practical combines a 30-day input window with a binary future-occurrence label. Its three catalogue channels, seven-day horizon and regional target are its own teaching task. The two examples above explain the decisions separately; they do not transfer results between the studies.

title: Sensitivity to initialization: map models
section: Prepare the experiment
text:
Prepare the experiment
We use small networks and three predeclared seeds: 7, 17 and 27. A seed controls pseudo-random choices used during initialization and optimization; variation across seeds is not uncertainty from observing a new earthquake catalogue. Retain every specified run.
The experiment evaluates validation only. The 2021–2025 period has already been inspected and is not an untouched test. Validation also controls early stopping, so its scores describe model development.

title: Sensitivity to initialization: map models
section: Turn events into daily inputs
text:
Turn events into daily inputs
Each day has three channels: log(1 + count), maximum magnitude excess above 4.5 (the daily maximum minus 4.5, or zero on an empty day), and an event-presence indicator. The regional series pools all locations. For the spatial tutorials we also keep six fixed geographic cells: three latitude bands by two longitude bands. Cell IDs run west to east within each row, then south to north. They are illustrative geographic bins, not inferred tectonic provinces; degree-based cells do not have identical physical areas. We retain the same domain and magnitude thresholds for every model.
Only training data should be used to judge whether the grid has adequate support. A finer map would create more rare targets, not automatically more useful information. X_regional supplies the regional models. The map and graph models use the six-cell arrays prepared from the same catalogue and calendar.

Code block 3 · Run the matching prepared-notebook cell in order. For self-study, copy into a new Colab code cell.

START = pd.Timestamp("2000-01-01", tz="UTC")
END = pd.Timestamp("2026-01-01", tz="UTC")  # exclusive
days = pd.date_range(START, END - pd.Timedelta(days=1), freq="D")
LAT_EDGES = np.array([-34.0, -32.0, -30.0, -28.0])
LON_EDGES = np.array([-74.0, -71.5, -69.0])
N_ROWS, N_COLS = 3, 2
FEATURES = ["log_count", "max_magnitude_excess", "has_event"]
inside = events.latitude.between(LAT_EDGES[0], LAT_EDGES[-1]) & events.longitude.between(LON_EDGES[0], LON_EDGES[-1])
selected = events.loc[inside & (events.time >= START) & (events.time < END) & (events.mag >= 4.5)].copy()
selected["day"] = (selected.time.dt.floor("D") - START).dt.days
selected["row"] = np.clip(np.searchsorted(LAT_EDGES, selected.latitude, side="right") - 1, 0, N_ROWS - 1)
selected["col"] = np.clip(np.searchsorted(LON_EDGES, selected.longitude, side="right") - 1, 0, N_COLS - 1)

counts = np.zeros((len(days), N_ROWS, N_COLS), dtype=np.float32)
max_excess = np.zeros_like(counts)
target_counts = np.zeros_like(counts)
indices = (selected.day.to_numpy(), selected.row.to_numpy(), selected.col.to_numpy())
np.add.at(counts, indices, 1)
np.maximum.at(max_excess, indices, selected.mag.to_numpy() - 4.5)
qualifying = selected.mag.to_numpy() >= 5.0
np.add.at(target_counts, tuple(axis[qualifying] for axis in indices), 1)
daily_grid_raw = np.stack([np.log1p(counts), max_excess, (counts > 0).astype(float)], axis=-1).astype("float32")
daily_regional_raw = np.stack([
    np.log1p(counts.sum(axis=(1, 2))),
    max_excess.max(axis=(1, 2)),
    (counts.sum(axis=(1, 2)) > 0).astype(float)
], axis=-1).astype("float32")
assert int(counts.sum()) == len(selected)
assert int(target_counts.sum()) == int(qualifying.sum())
print("Daily regional:", daily_regional_raw.shape, "; daily grid:", daily_grid_raw.shape)

Daily regional: (9497, 3) ; daily grid: (9497, 3, 2, 3)

title: Sensitivity to initialization: map models
section: Build histories, labels and chronological partitions
text:
Build histories, labels and chronological partitions
At each Monday origin t, inputs use [t − 30 days, t) and targets use [t, t + 7 days). We remove any target interval that crosses a train/validation/test boundary or the end of the catalogue. Inputs to a later partition can contain earlier historical days; their outcomes never enter training. Weekly target windows do not overlap, although histories overlap and earthquake sequences remain dependent.
The regional target is one binary outcome. The spatial target has six binary outcomes: several cells may be positive in the same week, or all may be zero. Six cell probabilities therefore need not sum to one.

Code block 4 · Run the matching prepared-notebook cell in order. For self-study, copy into a new Colab code cell.

LOOKBACK, HORIZON = 30, 7
VAL_START = pd.Timestamp("2017-01-01", tz="UTC")
TEST_START = pd.Timestamp("2021-01-01", tz="UTC")
regional_windows, grid_windows, grid_labels, kept_origins, partitions = [], [], [], [], []
excluded = []
for origin in pd.date_range("2001-01-01", "2025-12-31", freq="W-MON", tz="UTC"):
    i = (origin - START).days
    stop = origin + pd.Timedelta(days=HORIZON)
    split = "train" if origin < VAL_START else ("validation" if origin < TEST_START else "test")
    boundary = VAL_START if split == "train" else (TEST_START if split == "validation" else END)
    if i < LOOKBACK or stop > boundary:
        excluded.append(str(origin.date()))
        continue
    regional_windows.append(daily_regional_raw[i - LOOKBACK:i])
    grid_windows.append(daily_grid_raw[i - LOOKBACK:i])
    grid_labels.append((target_counts[i:i + HORIZON].sum(axis=0) > 0).astype("int32"))
    kept_origins.append(origin)
    partitions.append(split)
origins = pd.DatetimeIndex(kept_origins)
partitions = np.asarray(partitions)
raw_regional = np.stack(regional_windows)
raw_grid = np.stack(grid_windows)
y_grid = np.stack(grid_labels)
y_regional = y_grid.any(axis=(1, 2)).astype("int32")
train_mask = partitions == "train"
val_mask = partitions == "validation"
test_mask = partitions == "test"
assert np.all(origins[train_mask] + pd.Timedelta(days=HORIZON) <= VAL_START)
assert np.all(origins[val_mask] + pd.Timedelta(days=HORIZON) <= TEST_START)
assert np.all(origins[test_mask] + pd.Timedelta(days=HORIZON) <= END)
assert not np.any(train_mask & val_mask)
print("Windows:", dict(zip(*np.unique(partitions, return_counts=True))))
print("Excluded boundary/incomplete targets:", excluded)
display(pd.DataFrame({
    "cell": np.arange(N_ROWS * N_COLS),
    "row_south_to_north": np.repeat(np.arange(N_ROWS), N_COLS),
    "col_west_to_east": np.tile(np.arange(N_COLS), N_ROWS),
    "training_positive_weeks": y_grid[train_mask].sum(axis=0).reshape(-1),
    "training_base_rate": y_grid[train_mask].mean(axis=0).reshape(-1)
}))

title: Sensitivity to initialization: map models
section: Standardize using training histories only
text:
Standardize using training histories only
For regional inputs, we estimate one mean and standard deviation per channel. For spatial inputs, we also use one pair per channel, pooled across training cells, so the map and graph models receive exactly the same scaled arrays. A historical day can contribute to several overlapping training windows. These training estimates are applied to every validation history. Empty days remain distinguishable through the presence channel. Target labels are never standardized.
The metric function averages squared probability errors and binary log losses. On spatial outputs these are averages of marginal cell scores, not the likelihood of a joint spatial point process. We will also inspect each cell separately.

Code block 5 · Run the matching prepared-notebook cell in order. For self-study, copy into a new Colab code cell.

regional_mean = raw_regional[train_mask].mean(axis=(0, 1), dtype=np.float64)
regional_scale = raw_regional[train_mask].std(axis=(0, 1), dtype=np.float64)
regional_scale = np.where(regional_scale > 0, regional_scale, 1.0)
grid_mean = raw_grid[train_mask].mean(axis=(0, 1, 2, 3), dtype=np.float64)
grid_scale = raw_grid[train_mask].std(axis=(0, 1, 2, 3), dtype=np.float64)
grid_scale = np.where(grid_scale > 0, grid_scale, 1.0)
X_regional = ((raw_regional - regional_mean) / regional_scale).astype("float32")
X_grid = ((raw_grid - grid_mean) / grid_scale).astype("float32")
assert X_regional.shape[1:] == (30, 3) and X_grid.shape[1:] == (30, 3, 2, 3)
assert np.isfinite(X_regional).all() and np.isfinite(X_grid).all()

def score_probabilities(y_true, probability):
    y_true = np.asarray(y_true, dtype=float)
    probability = np.asarray(probability, dtype=float)
    assert y_true.shape == probability.shape
    assert np.isin(y_true, [0, 1]).all() and np.isfinite(probability).all()
    assert ((probability >= 0) & (probability <= 1)).all()
    clipped = np.clip(probability, 1e-7, 1 - 1e-7)
    return {"brier": float(np.mean((probability - y_true) ** 2)),
            "log_loss": float(-np.mean(y_true * np.log(clipped) + (1 - y_true) * np.log1p(-clipped)))}

protocol = {
    "tutorial": TUTORIAL, "seeds": SEEDS, "epochs_max": EPOCHS, "batch_size": BATCH_SIZE,
    "lookback_days": LOOKBACK, "horizon_days": HORIZON,
    "pack_url": PACK_URL, "pack_sha256": PACK_SHA256, "catalogue_sha256": CATALOGUE_SHA256,
    "features": FEATURES, "latitude_edges": LAT_EDGES.tolist(), "longitude_edges": LON_EDGES.tolist(),
    "train": "2001-2016", "validation": "2017-2020", "test": "2021-2025; not evaluated here",
    "historical_as_of_verified": False, "scope": "Exploratory retrospective; validation only",
    "regional_mean": regional_mean.tolist(), "regional_scale": regional_scale.tolist(),
    "grid_mean": grid_mean.tolist(), "grid_scale": grid_scale.tolist(),
    "python": platform.python_version(), "tensorflow": tf.__version__, "keras": keras.__version__,
    "numpy": np.__version__, "pandas": pd.__version__, "scikit_learn": sklearn.__version__
}
(RUN_DIR / "protocol.json").write_text(json.dumps(protocol, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
pd.DataFrame({"origin": origins.astype(str), "split": partitions}).to_csv(RUN_DIR / "windows.csv", index=False)
print("Ready:", X_regional.shape, X_grid.shape, "; no test outcomes used for fitting or evaluation.")
